question_text: Show that there is no real number k for which the equation x² − 3x + k = 0 has two distinct roots in [0, 1].

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you assume at the start, which theorem you apply, and where the contradiction appears.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Assume two roots and apply Rolle's theorem
steps.margin_note: First mark. Nothing here is computed. The mark is for the assumption plus the correct application of Rolle's theorem to the interval [α, β] formed by the two assumed roots.
steps.memory_tip: Two roots of the same function are two points with equal values, which is exactly the condition Rolle's theorem needs.
lines: Suppose, if possible, that for some real k the equation f(x) = 0 has two distinct roots α and β in [0, 1], with α < β.
f is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [α, β] and differentiable on (α, β).
Also f(α) = 0 and f(β) = 0, so f(α) = f(β).
All three conditions of Rolle's theorem hold, so there is a c in (α, β) with f′(c) = 0.

recall.must_convey: That we assume two distinct roots α, β in [0, 1] and apply Rolle's theorem on [α, β], since f(α) = f(β) = 0.

steps.why: The question asks you to show that something does NOT exist, and there is no k to compute, so the proof runs by contradiction: assume such a k exists and show the assumption cannot hold. Rolle's theorem is the right tool because two roots of the same function are two points with equal values.
common_mistakes: Trying to find a value of k instead of assuming one exists.
Using the discriminant 9 − 4k > 0 alone, which shows the roots are distinct but says nothing about where they lie.

steps.label: Reach the contradiction
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The chain (α, β) ⊆ (0, 1) is the line the proof depends on — without it, c = 3/2 is just a number and contradicts nothing.
steps.memory_tip: f′(x) = 2x − 3 is zero only at x = 3/2, and 3/2 is outside [0, 1]. That single fact is the whole proof.
lines: But 0 ≤ α < c < β ≤ 1, so c lies in (0, 1) and therefore c < 1.

lines.text: ∴ there is no real number k for which x² − 3x + k = 0 has two distinct roots in [0, 1]

recall.must_convey: That f′(c) = 0 forces c = 3/2, which cannot lie in (0, 1), so the assumption fails and no such k exists.

steps.why: The value c = 3/2 does not depend on k at all, which is why no choice of k can rescue the assumption. That is what makes the statement true for every real k rather than for most of them.
common_mistakes: Stating c = 3/2 without saying why c had to lie in (0, 1).
Concluding that k has no real value at all, when the claim is only about roots lying inside [0, 1].
